text.en: Scat syllables can copy instruments. A 1987 study likened Ella Fitzgerald's "b" and "p" to reed instruments and her "d" to tongued brass, and Sarah Vaughan's "sh" to brushes on a drum.

source.en: Wikipedia, Scat singing (citing Stewart, Jazzforschung/Jazz Research 19 (1987))

headline.en: Scat is singing like a horn on syllables. The band plays a call; you answer it. No wrong notes here: where you choose, every lit note fits.

detail.en: Any lit note: one that sounds at rest

text.en: Echo one call, its syllables written out.

Four trades. End each on any lit note, a different one each time if you like. Light and easy: a loose jaw, a medium volume, the middle of your voice. Accent with breath, never the throat. Stop if anything tightens.

measures.en: Scored on your notes on pitch and on the swung beat, each one you chose on a lit note.

text.en: Swing isn't one fixed ratio. When researchers measured jazz drummers' ride cymbals, the long note grew longer at slow tempos, up to about 3.5 to 1, and the swing evened out at fast tempos.

source.en: Friberg and Sundström, Jazz drummers' swing ratio in relation to tempo, Acoustical Society of America (1999)

headline.en: Swing is long, short: "doo-BAH". A soft d on the long note, a b and a little accent on the short one, with breath, never the throat.

text.en: The word "bebop" comes from scat syllables. In Dizzy Gillespie's account, fans heard him scat his new, untitled tunes to the band, and "would ask for bebop."

text.en: Louis Armstrong and His Hot Five recorded "Heebie Jeebies" in 1926, and it put scat singing on the map, though others had scatted on records before. Armstrong said he dropped his lyric sheet and scatted instead; historians still debate the story.

source.en: Riccardi, I Got the Heebies!, Louis Armstrong House Museum

text.en: In "stop-time" the band hits a chord, then falls silent for the soloist to fill. Louis Armstrong's famous stop-time chorus in "Potato Head Blues" (1927) drew partly on the tap dancing at the Sunset Café.

source.en: Wikipedia, Potato Head Blues (citing Brothers, Louis Armstrong: Master of Modernism (2014))

text.en: A jazz "shell voicing" leaves out a chord's fifth, sometimes its root too: the third and seventh alone imply what kind of chord it is. Bud Powell and Bill Evans used them extensively.

source.en: University of North Carolina Wilmington, Using Shell Voicings

text.en: The riff of Glenn Miller's "In the Mood" was going round the bands years earlier: Wingy Manone recorded it in "Tar Paper Stomp" in 1930, and Fletcher Henderson's band used it in 1931.

text.en: In his autobiography, W. C. Handy wrote that the flat third and seventh in his major-key blues came from the music of poor Black Southerners. Today we call them blue notes.

headline.en: The blue note is the flat third sung against a major chord: it rubs on purpose, then lifts to the third. No pushing on the bend.

text.en: At the 1956 Newport Jazz Festival, Paul Gonsalves soloed for 27 choruses in Duke Ellington's Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue. The seated crowd rose to dance, and the night revived Ellington's career.
